summary.title: How to Remember What You Read
summary.one_liner: Learn active reading habits, such as preparing context, taking notes with the Blank Sheet Method, marking up books, and applying ideas, so that what you read actually sticks.
keywords: how to remember what you read
takeaways: Consuming information is not the same as learning; reflection and feedback turn reading into usable knowledge.
Prepare before reading: choose books that interest or challenge you, gather historical or author context, and define your reason for reading.
Use the Blank Sheet Method: write what you know before reading, add notes in a different color after each session, and file the sheets in a binder to review.
Stay focused, mark up books, and link ideas to mental models such as confirmation bias, incentives, and survivorship bias.
Quit boring or bad books, apply lessons immediately, teach them to others, and keep notes in a searchable system.
summary.summary: This Farnam Street article argues that reading only pays off when you actively engage with the text and retain what you learn. It is organized into three parts: active reading (choosing books, getting context, knowing your purpose, skimming, matching books to your circumstances), remembering what you read (note taking with the author's Blank Sheet Method, focus, marking up books, making mental links with mental models, and stopping books you dislike, including Nancy Pearl's Rule of 50), and what to do afterward (applying lessons, the Feynman technique, and making notes searchable). It is a practical essay with quoted authors and suggested tools like index cards, commonplace books, and digital note systems.
